note: Watch-mode narration. Each segment carries its mission and anchor (event or phase, plus an offset in mission seconds). Built to public/narration/<version>/ by tools/narration/build.sh. Captions show the text exactly.

cues.text: This is the K-1, a two-stage rocket, standing on its launch pad.
Its tanks hold liquid oxygen and RP-1, a refined kerosene. A rocket carries its oxidizer as well as its fuel, because there is no air to burn where it is going.
The access arms swing back. The white vapor is liquid oxygen boiling at minus one hundred and eighty-three degrees Celsius. It is vented, and topped up, until the final minutes.
Engine start. A self-igniting fluid called T E A, T E B flashes green, the turbopumps spin up, and seven engines build thrust.
Clamps still hold the rocket down while the flight computers confirm that every engine is healthy.
Release, and liftoff. Five point two meganewtons of thrust lift about four hundred and forty tonnes, so the rocket accelerates slowly at first.
Tower cleared. The rocket now tips over, just slightly, toward the east.
From here it does not fight the air. It keeps its nose along the airflow and lets gravity bend its path into a curve: a gravity turn.
Heading east also borrows the Earth's own spin, about four hundred meters per second at this latitude.
The air is thinning, but the rocket is going faster. Dynamic pressure, half the air density times the speed squared, is at its peak.
This is the moment of greatest aerodynamic load, and the engines throttle back to ease through it.
Main engine cutoff. The first stage has used most of its propellant, keeping a reserve to fly itself home.
Stage separation. Pneumatic pushers ease the stages apart. Both are still climbing at the same speed; they drift apart gently.
The upper-stage engine lights once it is clear of the interstage. Its huge nozzle extension would not work at sea level. It is shaped for the near-vacuum up here.
Meanwhile, the booster has flipped around with small nitrogen thrusters, and relights three engines to head back toward the coast. You can follow it in the mission explorer.
Above about a hundred and ten kilometers, the air is too thin to heat or batter the satellite. The fairing halves swing open and fall away: carrying them higher would only waste propellant.
The upper stage now burns for several minutes, pointing more and more horizontally.
Orbit is not about height. It is about going sideways so fast, about seven point seven kilometers per second here, that the ground curves away as quickly as you fall.
Engine cutoff. The vehicle is in orbit. Nothing pushes it now, and it does not slow down. It is falling around the Earth.
This coast is shown sped up. The stage and its satellite keep moving at nearly eight kilometers per second, on a path set by gravity alone.
Payload separation. A clamp band lets go, and springs push the satellite gently away from the stage.
The satellite unfolds its solar arrays, turns them toward the Sun, and raises its antenna to contact the ground. The rocket's job is done.
A suborbital research flight uses the booster alone, with a capsule on top instead of an upper stage.
It carries a reduced propellant load: the goal is height, not orbital speed.
Engine start, and the hold-down clamps release when thrust is confirmed.
Liftoff. The rocket climbs almost straight up, tilted a little to the east so the capsule will come down over the ocean.
Engine cutoff, early. The booster has enough speed to throw the capsule above one hundred kilometers, and no more.
The capsule separates. From here both are simply coasting: rising, slowing, and about to fall back.
The capsule crosses one hundred kilometers, a common definition of the edge of space. Inside, experiments are in free fall.
The top of the arc. The capsule is barely moving sideways, so it cannot stay up here. Reaching space is not the same as staying in orbit.
Falling back, it gains speed again. With no sideways speed to spare, the path returns to Earth a few minutes after launch.
The heat shield leads. Entry from a suborbital arc is gentler than from orbit, but the capsule still meets the air at several times the speed of sound.
Drogue parachutes steady the capsule and slow it before the mains.
Main parachutes open in stages. Reefing lines hold each canopy partly closed at first, limiting the opening shock.
Splashdown, at a few meters per second. Recovery crews are on the way.
The booster has flown its own path back and lights its center engine for landing.
This mission carries a communications satellite toward geostationary orbit, thirty-five thousand seven hundred and eighty-six kilometers up.
The rocket will not take it all the way. Watch which vehicle performs each maneuver.
Liftoff. This time the booster is not recovered: the energy for a high orbit uses the propellant that would otherwise bring it home.
Maximum dynamic pressure, then the climb out of the dense air.
Stage separation, and the upper stage takes over.
The fairing falls away above the atmosphere.
First cutoff. The stage and satellite are in a low parking orbit, coasting around the Earth.
They coast until they reach the right point: the next burn must happen where the orbit crosses the equator, so the high point of the new orbit lies over the equator too.
Before the engine restarts, small thrusters nudge the stage forward. In free fall the propellant floats; this settles it over the tank outlets.
Restart. The upper-stage engine burns again, adding speed at the low point of the orbit.
Cutoff. The orbit now stretches from about two hundred kilometers to thirty-six thousand. This is a transfer orbit, not the final orbit.
The satellite separates. From here, the satellite's own engine does the rest.
The long climb to the high point takes about five hours, shown here greatly sped up. The satellite slows as it rises, trading speed for height.
At the high point the satellite fires its apogee engine, sideways, to raise the low point and to remove the tilt of the orbit.
In reality this takes several burns over days. It is shown here as one, as an explanation.
A crew capsule on the K-1. Above it, the abort tower: a solid rocket motor that can pull the capsule clear of a failing booster in seconds.
Liftoff, timed for the moment the launch site passes under the station's orbital plane. Launching into the right plane saves an expensive change of direction later.
Maximum dynamic pressure. The abort tower is ready throughout this phase.
Stage separation.
With the dense air behind, the abort tower is no longer needed. Its jettison motor carries it away.
Cutoff. The capsule is in orbit, lower than the station and some distance behind it.
The capsule separates from the upper stage and opens its solar arrays.
Why not point at the station and fly straight to it? Because pushing forward raises your orbit, and a higher orbit is slower. You would climb and fall behind.
Instead, the capsule stays lower, where orbits are faster, and catches up gradually. This phase is shown with long quiet intervals omitted.
A burn raises the high point of the orbit toward the station's altitude.
A second burn at the top rounds out the orbit just below and behind the station.
Final approach along the line toward the Earth's center, from below. Here orbital motion helps: small thrusts, holds at fixed distances, and a closing speed of a few centimeters per second.
Soft capture. Latches catch the docking ring, and springs absorb the remaining motion.
Hard capture. Hooks pull the two vehicles into an airtight seal. Delivery complete.
The capsule undocks and backs away from the station with small thruster firings.
The deorbit burn. The service module's engine fires against the direction of travel.
Losing about a hundred meters per second is enough: the low point of the orbit now dips into the atmosphere.
The service module is no longer needed. It separates, and will burn up. Only the capsule, with its heat shield, is built to survive what comes next.
Entry interface, about a hundred and twenty kilometers up. The capsule meets the air at nearly eight kilometers per second, heat shield first.
Peak heating. The shock layer in front of the shield glows at thousands of degrees.
The ablative shield chars and slowly erodes, carrying heat away as it does, while the structure behind it stays cool.
The air takes away the orbital energy. The crew feel several times their normal weight.
Drogue parachutes stabilize the capsule and slow it.
Three main parachutes open, reefed at first, then fully.
Splashdown in the Atlantic. The mission ends where it began: on Earth, a short way from the launch site.
This rocket carries a small probe to fly past the Moon. It will not stop there: a flyby, not an orbit.
Liftoff.
Stage separation. The booster is expended on this mission.
The upper stage reaches a parking orbit and coasts, waiting for the right moment to leave.
Settling thrusters push the propellant to the back of the tanks before the restart.
Trans-lunar injection. The engine burns for several minutes, raising the speed to nearly eleven kilometers per second.
Cutoff. The probe is now on a long, stretched path that reaches out to the Moon's distance.
The probe separates. From here it coasts: no engine is running, yet it is moving the whole time.
Three days of coasting, shown greatly sped up. Earth's gravity slows the probe as it climbs away.
The probe crosses into the region where the Moon's gravity dominates. Seen from the Moon, it is now falling toward it.
Closest approach, over the far side. The Moon bends the probe's path and swings it onward.
Leaving the Moon's sphere of influence on an outbound trajectory. A flyby changes direction and speed without an engine burn, but to stay in lunar orbit the probe would have had to brake.
